returning although nobody notified. The standard and POSIX both allow it, so a wait that assumes a notification is wrong. A

is a notification sent while nobody was waiting: a condition variable stores nothing, so that notification is gone, and a thread that waits afterwards waits for a second one that may never come. The predicate stops both. On a spurious wake-up it is false and the wait loops; before the first wait it is already true, so the planner never waits at all.
Because the predicate reads the shared state, and reading it while the loader writes it is a data race. Holding the mutex also closes the window between the check and the wait:

c.v: You pass with the predicate form of

without a predicate and then explaining the two problems correctly is a partial pass. A wait with no mutex, or a predicate that reads the state without one, is a fail: it is the bug this topic exists to remove.
A condition variable is a waiting room for threads. A thread that cannot make progress until some shared state changes goes to sleep on it, and a thread that changes that state wakes it up.
is that waiting room, and it always works with a
that guards the state, and with a
, a small function that returns whether the state the waiter wants is now true.

The problem it solves is the cost of asking again. Without it a waiting thread spins, testing a flag in a loop and burning a core while it does. I measured the two: a thread spinning on an atomic flag for half a second used 0.47 seconds of processor time, the same wait on a condition variable used 0.00, both finishing in the same half second of wall clock. On a robot with a control loop and four sensor threads, a spinner is a core stolen from the work.
The mechanism has three parts, and all three are needed. The writer changes the state while holding the mutex, then calls

releases the mutex, sleeps until a notification, and takes the mutex again before it returns. The predicate is what makes the loop correct, because a wait can return without a notification, which is called a spurious wake-up, and because a notification sent before anyone was waiting is not stored anywhere, which is called a lost wake-up. The predicate turns both into a test of the state instead of a test of the notification.
What it costs is that every waiter shares one queue. If threads on one condition variable are waiting for different things,
can wake a thread whose predicate is false, which goes back to sleep while the thread that could have run is never woken. The fixes are
, or one condition variable per condition, which is what the bounded queue does next.
You meet it in the robot whenever one thread hands work to another: a map loaded before planning starts, a monitor waiting for the next heartbeat, a worker waiting for the next command.

subs.title: Condition variables, predicates and wait loops

c.v: A loader reads the map, two planners wait for it, and none of them spins:

blocks.text:
planner 0 got warehouse with 4000000 cells
planner 1 got warehouse with 4000000 cells

c.v: is a queue of sleeping threads and nothing else. It holds no value, remembers no notification, and knows nothing about what the threads are waiting for. All the knowledge lives in the state next to it, here
, which the mutex guards. That is why the three always appear together in one class, and why a condition variable on its own is never the answer to anything.

). Read it in that expanded form and the whole design follows. The predicate is evaluated first, with the mutex held, so a waiter that arrives after the map is loaded returns at once and never sleeps. If it is false, plain

releases the mutex and goes to sleep as one indivisible step, which is the part you could not write yourself with a mutex and a flag. When it wakes, it takes the mutex again before returning, so the predicate is tested under the lock every time. The loop means a wake-up that turns out to be worthless costs a test and another sleep.

The writer's side has its own order. Change the state with the mutex held, release the mutex, then notify. Changing the state under the mutex is what stops a race with the predicate. Notifying after the release is a small optimisation: a waiter woken while the writer still holds the mutex would wake up and immediately block on the mutex instead, so it goes back to sleep once more for no reason (
calls holding the lock during the notification a pessimisation). It is not a correctness question, and there is one case where holding it matters, which the failure step covers.

is right and cheaper, because it avoids a crowd of threads waking to fight over one mutex. If the waiters are waiting for different conditions, or if one change lets several of them proceed, as a one-shot flag does, you need

The timed waits come in the same two shapes.

What all this buys you is the processor time you would otherwise burn asking. A planner that spins on an atomic flag for half a second and one that waits on a condition variable for the same half second, both measured with

blocks.text:
spin on an atomic flag:   wall 0.51 s, user 0.47 s, sys 0.00 s
wait on a condition:      wall 0.53 s, user 0.00 s, sys 0.00 s

c.v: The waiting version uses no measurable processor time, because the kernel takes the thread off the run queue and puts it back when the notification comes. The spinning version keeps a core busy for the whole wait. On a robot that is a core the control loop no longer has, and on a battery it is watts. This is
, "don't wait without a condition", read from the other side: express the wait as a condition and the system can give the processor to somebody else.

Two more facts to carry into an interview. The permission to wake without a notification is what lets an implementation take the cheapest wake-up path it has, which is why the standard grants it and why the predicate is not optional. And a notification costs little while nobody waits: glibc builds condition variables on futexes, so
with nobody asleep is an atomic update rather than a system call.

The Test Bench monitor watches a heartbeat and reports a gap. Here it is as a handshake: the publisher hands over one sequence number at a time and waits until the monitor has taken it, and the monitor waits up to 100 ms for the next one. Two conditions, so two condition variables:

blocks.text:
monitor got beat 1
monitor got beat 2
monitor got beat 3
monitor saw no beat for 100 ms
publisher sent 3 beats, monitor reported 1 gap

items.v: There are two conditions here, "a beat is pending" and "the slot is free", so there are two condition variables. Each one has exactly one kind of waiter, which is why
is correct for both. One shared condition variable would work only with
, and every notification would wake a thread that has nothing to do.
The output is the same on every run, and two separate things make it so. The handshake fixes the order: the publisher cannot run ahead, because

is empty. The margin fixes the gap count: a beat has to reach the monitor inside 100 ms or the run gains a line, and the three handovers together took 421 to 546 microseconds over six runs, so each wait has more than two orders of magnitude of slack. A deadline set close to the work it waits for would make the output depend on how busy the machine is, and no amount of correct locking would save it. Given a queue instead of a single slot, the monitor might also see the beats in bursts, and the count of lines would depend on timing again. That is the difference the next topic is about.
, not a sentinel sequence number and not a bool plus an out-parameter. No value means "no beat within 100 ms", which is the monitor's whole job to detect.
Both notifications are sent after the enclosing block has released the lock. The inner braces are there for that: they end the

times, so it asks once more after the publisher has stopped, and that last call is the gap. A real monitor loops until its stop token is set, and then the number of gaps depends on how long the program runs.
Nothing here is a queue yet: the publisher blocks while the monitor is slow, and one beat waiting is the whole buffer. A bounded queue is this class with room for
items, which is why its members look familiar.

c.v: is there to keep the demonstration finishable. A real program writes
and waits until somebody kills it, with the flag it needed sitting true the whole time. The predicate version returns at once, without sleeping once, because
tests the predicate before it does anything else. That is the rule: the condition variable is the doorbell, the state is the door, and you look at the door.
The second failure is the spurious wake-up, which is the same fix from the other direction.
. The standard allows it and POSIX allows it for

explains that allowing it makes the implementation faster on some systems). One everyday route to it is a woken waiter that loses the mutex to a thread that was never waiting, and so finds the state already taken. The consequence is short: a bare
tells you nothing about the state, so never act on the fact that it returned. With the predicate form you never notice spurious wake-ups at all.
The third failure changes the state without the mutex. This code looks like it is doing the same job:
It is a data race on

and notifies in that instant. The notification arrives before the waiter is in the queue, so nobody hears it, and the waiter then sleeps on a condition that is already true. With the mutex held, the writer cannot be in that instant: the waiter is either still holding the mutex, and the writer waits, or it is already inside
, which released the mutex only once it was queued.

The fourth failure is a notification that goes to the wrong thread. Suppose one condition variable, some threads waiting for "the queue has an item" and others for "the queue has room", and the code calls

after taking an item out. The implementation may wake a consumer, whose predicate is false, so it goes straight back to sleep, while the producer waiting for room is never woken. Nothing is lost forever if more events follow, but under a steady load it shows up as a program that pauses for no reason, and with the last item it can stop for good. There are two fixes, and the bounded queue in the next topic uses the second: call
, which costs a thundering herd of threads waking to take one mutex in turn, or give each condition its own condition variable, so that every waiter on a queue is waiting for the same thing and
The fifth failure is about lifetime. Destroying a

while a thread is blocked on it is undefined behaviour, and so is destroying the mutex. The standard's only concession is that you may destroy the condition variable once every waiter has been notified, even if they have not yet run (
). In practice this means the object that owns the condition variable has to outlive every thread that waits on it, which the

-in-a-scope pattern gives you at no cost, as long as the object is declared before the threads. A class that owns both the threads and the condition variable must stop and join the threads in its destructor, before its own members are destroyed; a member
declared last does that for you.

The last one is not a bug but a habit worth having. Notifying while holding the mutex costs the woken thread a second sleep, because it wakes into a mutex the notifier still owns. Release first, then notify. The exception is the case where the notifier is about to destroy the state, or where the waiter's predicate reads something the notifier is still changing; then the notification belongs inside the lock, and the cost is one extra context switch.

c.v: notifies outside the lock for the reason the theory gave: a waiter woken while the counter still holds the mutex would wake into a blocked mutex. It notifies only on the transition to zero because that is the only moment any predicate changes from false to true. A notification at count 3 would wake every waiter to find
, test false and sleep again. Watching for the transition rather than the state is the shape to remember: compute the change under the lock, act on it outside.
